overview.headline: Building geologic time from relative order to radiometric age

keyPoints.point: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, a span that shows the scale of deep time.
keyPoints.quote: Earth is 4.54 billion years old, a span of time that is hard for many people to grasp.

keyPoints.point: The law of superposition shows older rocks on bottom and younger rocks on top for relative time.
keyPoints.quote: The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.

keyPoints.point: Uniformitarianism states present Earth processes shaped Earth in the past and will shape the future.
keyPoints.quote: the processes that we see happening on Earth today are the same processes that shaped Earth in the past

keyPoints.point: A half-life is the time for half the parent isotopes to decay to daughter isotope.
keyPoints.quote: A half-life is the length of time it takes for half of the number of original, or parent, isotopes to decay to a stable daughter isotope.

keyPoints.point: Lead-lead dating of the Canyon Diablo meteorite gave an age near 4.55 billion years for Earth.
keyPoints.quote: used lead-lead dating to determine that the Canyon Diablo meteorite was 4.55 billion years old.

keyTerms.gloss: geological concept for vast Earth history that is hard to grasp
keyTerms.quote: One of the distinctive characteristics of geological thinking is the concept of deep time.

keyTerms.gloss: law that older rocks lie below younger rocks indicating relative time
keyTerms.quote: The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.

keyTerms.gloss: principle that present processes shaped past geology and continue into future
keyTerms.quote: In 1788, James Hutton proposed what would become the foundational principle of geology — uniformitarianism.

keyTerms.gloss: law that extinct species are replaced in consistent fossil order
keyTerms.quote: In 1815, Smith developed the law of faunal succession, which states that species become extinct and are replaced by new species
